title: Dynamic Resolution
summary: Dynamic Resolution is the umbrella for techniques in which malware does not carry a fixed destination but computes one at run time. The implant and the adversary's infrastructure share an algorithm, so the same inputs produce the same domain, address or port on both sides, leaving no hard coded indicator for defenders to block. This defeats static blocklists and domain seizures, and it supports fallback channels: when the primary server is unreachable, the implant keeps computing new candidates until one answers. Because the resolution step happens on the client, telemetry is behavioural rather than signature based. It appears as bursts of non resolving lookups, high volumes of Domain Name System (DNS) queries from a host with no such business need, requests to algorithmically similar names, or connections to addresses and ports derived by arithmetic instead of ordinary name resolution. Defenders separate this from legitimate activity by baselining domain entropy and query failure rates per host, watching for many failed lookups that end in one success, and correlating the responding address with reputation, registration age and certificate data.

beginner.definition: This is a family of tricks where malware works out its own contact address instead of storing one. The malware and the attacker's servers run the same recipe, so both sides agree on an address without talking first. Blocking a single address does not help, because a new one appears. The hidden control channel therefore stays alive.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you block one bad address, a static program simply fails and stops. Dynamic resolution means the program can find a new address on its own. That makes blocking and taking down attacker servers much harder for defenders. You have to look at patterns instead, such as one computer making many failed name lookups.
howItWorks: The attacker builds a program and a matching server setup that use the same calculation method.
That calculation takes changing inputs, such as the date, a hidden number or a list of words.
The program produces a domain name, an address or a port, and then tries to contact it.
If nothing answers, the program works out the next result from the same calculation and retries.
The attacker prepares or registers only the few results that the program is likely to reach.
Defenders see the failed attempts as an unusual pattern of name lookups from one host.
beginner.example: Think of two friends who agree on a rule instead of a fixed meeting place. On Monday they meet at the seventh bench, on Tuesday at the eighth. Anyone watching one bench sees nothing at all. The friends always find each other, because they both know the rule and the date. Malware that calculates its own contact address behaves in exactly that way.
takeaways: Static blocklists cannot stop a destination that is calculated fresh each time.
A burst of failed name lookups from one host is an early warning worth investigating.
Defences should focus on behaviour and patterns, not only on known bad addresses.

objectives: Explain what dynamic resolution means and why a fixed blocklist is not enough.
Describe how a shared algorithm lets both sides agree on a destination without contact.
Identify the DNS and network telemetry that dynamic resolution produces.
Explain how fallback channels keep command and control alive after disruption.
Describe how to baseline normal name lookup behaviour for hosts in your network.
